Abstract

  Multiple Phospholipase D (PLD) genes have been identi®ed in plants and encode isoforms with
distinct regulatory and catalytic properties. Elucidation of the genetic and biochemical heterogeneity has
provided  important  clues  as  to  the  regulation  and  function  of   this  family  of  enzymes.
Polyphosphoinositides, Ca2+, and G-proteins are possible cellular regulators for PLD activation. PLD-
mediated hydrolysis of membrane lipids increases in response to various stresses. Recent studies suggest
that PLD  plays a  role  in  the  signaling and  production  of hormones  involved  in  plant  stress
responses. 7 2000 Elsevier Science Ltd. All rights reserved.

1. Introduction


  Phospholipase D (PLD) was ®rst discovered in plants about half a century ago and was
subsequently found in animals, fungi, and bacteria [49,50]. This enzyme is widespread in the
plant kingdom [102]. Earlier studies generated considerable information about  its catalytic
properties, and one most notable feature is its need of millimolar Ca2+ for activity in vitro
[50]. This and other perplexing properties of the conventional PLD raised many questions as
well as doubts concerning its cellular signi®cance and regulation [105].
  This enzyme has received renewed attention in recent years, partly due to the realization of
the  roles  of phospholipases and membrane  lipids  in  cell  regulation and  function. PLD
hydrolyzes glycerol-phospholipids at the terminal phosphodiesteric bond, producing PA and a
free hydrophilic head group (Fig. 1). It also can transfer the phosphatidyl moiety to primary
alcohols to form phosphatidylalcohol, through a process referred to as transphosphatidylation
(Fig.  1). These  activities potentially have a profound impact on membrane structure and
stability, because phospholipids form the matrix of biological membranes. In addition, recent
studies have shown that activation of PLD produces secondary messengers. PLD is involved in
a wide variety of cellular and physiological processes, including phytohormone action, vesicular
tracking,  secretion,  cytoskeletal  arrangements,  meiosis, tumor  promotion,  pathogenesis,
membrane deterioration, and senescence [10,14,29,41,42,51,57,84,103,104,125].
  The  application  of  molecular  biological  investigations  has   facilitated  greatly  the

This has also provided means to characterize the expression and regulation of PLD genes and

isoenzymes. Delineation of the potential genetic redundancy and unique functions of the
multiple PLDs may hold the key to a comprehensive understanding of the PLD family. This
article will highlight the progress made since 1993 towards elucidation of the molecular basis,
regulation, and function of the multiple PLDs in plants. Readers are referred to other reviews
for the earlier work on PLD and on plant phospholipases in general [19,50,84,125].

2. Molecular analysis of multiple phospholipase Ds and genes

2.1. cDNA cloning and sequence comparison of multiple PLDs

2.1.1. Cloning of multiple PLDs
  An intracellular PLD was cloned ®rst from castor bean in 1994 [128]. The cDNA cloning
was preceded by determination of the N-terminal amino acid sequence of a PLD puri®ed from
castor bean endosperm [126]. The identity of the cDNA as PLD was established by expressing
a catalytically active PLD from this clone in Escherichia coli. Subsequently, three Arabidopsis
EST cDNA clones were found to share a signi®cant sequence similarity to the castor bean
PLD. One EST clone displayed about 70% sequence identity to the cloned castor bean PLD,
and the other two showed about 40% sequence identity. Full length cDNAs for the three PLD
cDNAs were isolated from Arabidopsis by employing a combination of rapid ampli®cation of
5'-cDNA ends (5'-RACE), nested PCR, and screening of cDNA libraries [35,91,100]. The
names PLDa, b, and g were based on the order of cloning from Arabidopsis [100]. A fourth
PLD cDNA has been cloned recently from Arabidopsis and is named PLDg2 because of the
close identity of  its sequence to that of PLDg (now PLDg1)  [101]. The amino acid and
nucleotide sequences of PLDb and the two PLDgs are related more closely to each other than
to PLDa. PLDb and gs are approximately 65% identical at the amino acid sequence level and
are about 40% identical to Arabidopsis PLDa. Multiple PLDs now have been cloned from
three other species; two PLDs have been cloned in rice, cabbage [89], and C. plantagineum
(Fig. 2; Table 1) [117].

2.2.2. Promoter analysis
  The availability of the 5'-¯anking region of these PLD genes allows analysis of cis- and
trans-elements  controlling  their  gene  promoter  activity and  expression. The  5'-¯anking
sequence of the castor bean PLD gene was searched for potential binding sites of various
transcription  factors  and  transcriptional  regulatory  elements   [136].  Primer  extension
experiments were conducted to determine the transcription initiation site. Most of the potential
sites for transcriptional regulation reside in the region from nucleotides ÿ1199 to ÿ730. The
hexamer ACGTCA at nucleotide 1175 appears to be a core element. Hexamer or hexamer-like
boxes exist in the cis-control region of numerous plant genes known to be regulated by various
environmental and physiological signals. Indeed, deletion of the region from nucleotides ÿ1199
to ÿ731 led to a complete loss of the function of the PLD gene promoter, con®rming that
sequences within the 5'-¯anking region are crucial for the basal and regulated expression of the
PLD gene.
  Comparison of the predicted promoter regions of the Arabidopsis PLD and two rice genes
with the castor bean promoter did not reveal signi®cant sequence similarity. Two regions
within the predicted rice PLD1 gene promoter showed similarity to several promoter sequences
in the database [81]. One segment was similar to the promoter region of a gene for serine
carboxypeptidase and  the other was  similar  to  the promoter region  of a  rice gene  for
phenylalanine ammonia lyase. However, the sequence of the predicted promoter region of
PLD2 did not display signi®cant similarity to other reported sequences [81]. The role of the

2.3. Domain structures of PLD proteins

2.3.1. Catalytic, duplicated HKD motifs
  The PLDs cloned from eukaryotes all contain two HxKxxxD motifs (Fig. 4) [63,98]. They
are separated by approximately 320 amino acids in plant PLDs. The absolute conservation of
these amino acids suggests that his, lys, and asp at these positions are active site residues. The
necessity of these residues for PLD activity has been documented by site-speci®c mutagenesis
in yeast PLD; changes in one of the residues led to the loss of PLD activity [114]. The

3. Properties of multiple PLDS identi®ed in plant extracts

6. Regulation and activation mechanisms


6.1. Regulation at the gene and protein levels

6.1.1. PLD gene expression as a control of PLD activity
  The conventional PLD activity is present in nearly all plant tissues. If not tightly regulated,
this enzyme may have a drastic eect on membrane lipid degradation. One such example is the
loss of phospholipids during homogenization of some plant tissues [49,50]. The massive PLD-
mediated hydrolysis may be viewed as a consequence of deregulation of PLD resulting from
cell  disruption. Therefore, mechanisms must  exist to control or sequester PLD from  its
substrates in vivo.
  Current data indicate that the cellular regulation of PLD is complex and involves several
mechanisms, some of which are long-term and some short-term  controls. The long-term
regulation refers to the change in levels of PLD protein that could result from combined
activities of gene expression, protein synthesis, and degradation. The promoter and RNA
analyses discussed earlier indicate that gene expression plays an important role in regulating
PLD activity. A high PLDa activity is often associated with a high level of PLD mRNA and
protein in conditions such as, seed germination, leaf development, and treatments with ABA,
ethylene, and pathogens [42,110,136]. PLDa protein appears to be quite stable; substantial
PLD protein was present even when the PLD mRNA level became undetectable [42]. On the
other hand, increased PLD degradation during senescence was implicated as a reason for the
relatively low PLDa concentration in castor bean leaves [107]. However, no study has directly
measured the rate of PLD synthesis and degradation, and thus, the turnover rate of PLD is
unknown.

7. Cellular functions of PLD

  Cellular functions of PLD and phospholipases may be considered in three general categories:
lipid degradation, cellular regulation (such as, signal transduction), and membrane remodeling.
Most early functional studies on plant PLD dealt with the role of PLD in lipid catabolism and
membrane  deterioration  during  senescence,  ageing,  and  stress  injuries  [13,50,116]. The
functional studies of PLD in recent years, however, have centered on  its participation in
cellular regulation via transmembrane signaling [19,84,125]. The role of PLD in membrane
remodeling and homeostasis is largely unexplored.

8. Perspectives

  The biochemical and molecular knowledge of PLD has increased greatly over the last several
years. The identi®cation and cloning of distinct plant PLDs have opened new doors to further
the investigation of PLD. Seven PLD genes have already been identi®ed. When the entire
Arabidopsis genome is sequenced, more PLD genes would probably be revealed in the plant.
The structural and genetic heterogeneity of PLD may play a vital role in regulating its cellular
functions. Increasing evidence has pointed to a role of PLD in signaling cascades, secretion,
and other regulatory processes. It is also important to note that PLD can participate in other
processes, including membrane degradation and remodeling. Dierent PLDs could be involved
in a speci®c cellular process and, conversely, an individual PLD could have multiple functions.

insights into the possible roles of PLD in speci®c physiological processes. But many questions
are unanswered with regard to the function and regulation of PLD in the cell. The question of
whether PLD  is an essential enzyme or  is required for a speci®c cellular or physiological
process in plants remains. The challenge in addressing such a question has become obvious
with the discovery of multiple PLD genes in plants and other organisms. Another key question
is: what are the molecular and cellular mechanisms by which PLD executes its cellular eects?
An answer to this question requires identi®cation of cellular targets of PLD activation and
factors that  interact with PLD. The lack of information on the  cellular eects of  lipid
messengers in general is the major impediment in plant lipid-signaling research. However, the
current  ®eld  of PLD  is poised  for major developments because many important  tools,
including the cloned PLDs, speci®c  antibodies, transgenic  plants, genetic knockouts, and
functional genomics,  are now becoming  available  to address  these  questions. Continued
